title: Plugins
description: How to package, distribute, and install Claude Code extensions: manifest, marketplaces, dependencies, and scope management.

articles.title: A self-contained, versionable, shareable directory
articles.summary: What a plugin can package and when it's worth converting .claude/ configuration into one

subsections.title: From standalone configuration to a plugin

blocks.content: A Claude Code plugin is a self-contained directory that packages extensions to distribute them as a single versioned unit, instead of configuring each piece separately in `.claude/`. Official docs recommend the opposite of what intuition suggests: start with standalone configuration in `.claude/` to iterate quickly, and only convert it into a plugin once it's ready to share.

items.title: Namespacing
items.description: A plugin's skills are invoked as `/plugin-name:skill-name`, avoiding name collisions between different plugins.

items.title: Composable
items.description: A single plugin can bundle skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, LSP servers, monitors, themes, and workflows all at once.

items.title: Versionable
items.description: It has its own metadata manifest and can be published to a marketplace, unlike a `.claude/settings.json` file that isn't versioned as an independent unit.

rows: The modern way to extend behavior — Claude invokes them automatically
Connection to external tools and data via Model Context Protocol
Code intelligence — requires the language server binary to already be installed on the machine
Legacy way to extend behavior — skills is the modern replacement

subsections.title: When it's worth making the jump to a plugin

blocks.content: The official recommendation to start in `.claude/` and only migrate once it's ready to share has a concrete reason: while content lives loose in `.claude/`, every iteration is just editing a file and testing again. Packaging it into a plugin too early adds the manifest, versioning, and eventually a marketplace — coordination costs that aren't worth paying while behavior is still being tuned.

blocks.title: The signal that it's time to migrate
blocks.content: When a second person or a second repo needs the same skill, hook, or MCP server, keeping loose copies in each `.claude/` means a fix made in one place never reaches the other. A versioned plugin with a marketplace solves that: update once, propagate to everyone who installed it.

articles.title: Structure of .claude-plugin/plugin.json
articles.summary: The one required field, semver versioning, and how manifest paths replace or merge with default locations

blocks.content: The manifest lives at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` inside the plugin directory. The only required field is `name` (kebab-case) — it doubles as the unique identifier and as the namespace prefix for its skills.

rows: Human-readable name in the plugin manager (falls back to `name` if missing)
Semver (`major.minor.patch`). If omitted, Claude Code derives it from the git SHA or the source command
Custom paths for each content type — see below
If `false`, the plugin starts disabled until the user manually enables it
Other required plugins — see the dependencies section
Interactive configuration schema the user fills in on install

blocks.title: Replaces or merges depending on the field
blocks.content: A path in `skills`, `mcpServers`, or `lspServers` adds to the default location instead of replacing it; a path in `commands` or `agents` instead fully replaces the search in its default location. `hooks` has its own merge rules. If a field is left out entirely, Claude Code looks in that content type's default location inside the plugin.

blocks.title: Paths are relative to the plugin's directory, not the project's
blocks.content: Any path declared in `plugin.json` (custom or default) resolves relative to the plugin's own root, not the project it ends up installed in — an easy detail to get wrong if you copy a path while thinking of the project's `.claude/` layout instead of the plugin's own.

articles.title: Plugin catalogs and how to install from them
articles.summary: The structure of marketplace.json, the seven source types a plugin can use, and the commands to add a marketplace and install

blocks.content: A marketplace is a catalog — a `marketplace.json` file listing available plugins. The user adds it once and then installs individual plugins from it.

rows: The plugin lives in the same repo as the marketplace
The most common case for public plugins
The plugin is a subdirectory inside a larger repo (sparse clone)
Distributing the plugin as an npm package
Direct distribution with integrity verification via `sha256`
The plugin is generated dynamically by running a command — never auto-installed as a dependency, see below
Registers a marketplace from the session
List, remove, or refresh the catalog
Installs while explicitly pinning the scope

blocks.title: Two official Anthropic marketplaces
blocks.content: `claude-plugins-official` (curated by Anthropic, registered automatically) and `anthropics/claude-plugins-community` (community, added manually with `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community`). Any other marketplace is third-party — see the security section below before adding one.

articles.title: Dependencies between plugins
articles.summary: How they're declared, what happens when one is missing, the cross-marketplace restriction, and the bundling pattern for team packages

blocks.content: A plugin can declare dependencies on other plugins in its manifest's `dependencies` field, using standard semver ranges (`~2.1.0`, `^2.0`, `>=1.4`).

blocks.title: The exception that breaks auto-install
blocks.content: When you install a plugin, its dependencies are resolved and installed automatically — except when a dependency uses a `command` source. In that case the user has to install it manually first; Claude Code never runs that source implicitly as part of resolving another plugin's dependencies.

If a dependency is missing, Claude Code disables the plugin and reports the `dependency-unsatisfied` error — both on load and when trying to enable it, along with instructions to install the missing dependency.

For security, a plugin can't depend on another one published in a different marketplace unless the source marketplace explicitly allows it via `allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn`. This prevents an untrusted marketplace from injecting dependencies toward arbitrary packages in another catalog.

blocks.title: A plugin can be nothing but a dependency bundle
blocks.content: A plugin with no content of its own, made entirely of a `dependencies` array, works as a team package: installing it installs the whole set at once. For version resolution to work, releases must be tagged in git as `{plugin-name}--v{version}` (e.g. `deploy-kit--v3.1.0`), typically via `claude plugin tag --push`.

subsections.title: The same four scopes as the rest of the configuration

rows: The whole team, committed to the repo
Only that user on that project, gitignored
Enforced by an admin, read-only for the user

blocks.title: Consistent with the rest of this site
blocks.content: It's the same scope hierarchy already documented in Permissions and in the hooks source table (user / project / local / plugin) — installing a plugin with `--scope project` instead of `user` is the difference between "only on my machine" and "the whole team gets it when they clone the repo."

articles.title: Trust, sandboxing, and what isn't guaranteed
articles.summary: Why installing a plugin from a third-party marketplace is a trust decision, not an operation verified by Anthropic

rows.value: Anthropic decides which plugins to include
No documented cryptographic signing or manual audit
Community goes through automated security screening; third-party marketplaces, none
Anthropic explicitly documents that it doesn't control or verify that the MCP servers, files, or other software bundled in a plugin work as advertised

blocks.title: No OS sandbox
blocks.content: Plugins don't run inside an OS sandbox — unlike Managed Agents, which do. A plugin can make network requests with no restriction imposed by the plugin mechanism itself. Installing one is, in terms of risk surface, equivalent to running third-party code with your own permissions.

items.title: Workspace trust
items.description: Plugins with project-level skill-dir scope only load after the user explicitly trusts the workspace.

items.title: MCP at project scope
items.description: Requires explicit approval per server — it doesn't auto-enable just by cloning the repo.

items.title: Monitors at project scope
items.description: Don't load at all, for security reasons — only available at the user scope.

items.title: strictPluginOnlyCustomization
items.description: An organization-level setting that forces every skill, agent, hook, and MCP server to come only from managed plugins — blocking individual customization via the user's own `.claude/`.
